headings.title: Introduction and Pathophysiology of Haemostasis
headings.content: Haemostasis is the dynamic, highly regulated physiological process that stops bleeding at the site of vascular injury while maintaining blood in a fluid state throughout the rest of the circulatory system. Understanding haemostasis is crucial for nursing students in Nigeria, as it forms the foundational baseline for managing patients with various bleeding and thrombotic disorders. The process occurs in two main phases: primary and secondary haemostasis, followed eventually by fibrinolysis. Primary haemostasis involves the interaction between damaged vascular endothelium, circulating platelets, and von Willebrand factor. When a blood vessel is injured, local vasoconstriction immediately reduces blood flow to the area. Simultaneously, subendothelial collagen is exposed, prompting platelets to adhere, become activated, and aggregate together to form a primary, albeit fragile, platelet plug. Secondary haemostasis involves the coagulation cascade, a complex series of enzymatic reactions involving clotting factors synthesized primarily by the liver. The cascade is traditionally divided into the intrinsic, extrinsic, and common pathways, culminating in the conversion of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that stabilize and strengthen the weak platelet plug into a solid blood clot. Finally, fibrinolysis is the regulated breakdown of the fibrin meshwork by plasmin to restore normal blood flow once tissue healing is underway. Any disruption in vasoconstriction, platelet function, clotting factors, or fibrinolytic control mechanisms can result in excessive hemorrhage or abnormal thrombosis, challenging the nurse's ability to maintain patient hemodynamic stability.

headings.title: Classification and Etiology of Bleeding Disorders
headings.content: Bleeding disorders are a diverse group of clinical conditions characterized by a tendency to hemorrhage excessively due to abnormalities in blood vessels, platelets, or coagulation factors. To provide effective nursing care in Nigerian clinical settings, nurses must categorize these disorders based on their etiology and pathophysiology into inherited and acquired forms. Inherited bleeding disorders are typically genetic mutations passed down through generations, affecting the production or function of specific clotting proteins or von Willebrand factor. Examples include Haemophilia A and B, which are X-linked recessive conditions, and von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder. On the other hand, acquired bleeding disorders develop later in life due to underlying medical conditions, systemic illnesses, nutritional deficiencies, or drug therapies. Common examples encountered in medical-surgical wards include disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, and anticoagulant therapy complications like warfarin overdose. Furthermore, vascular defects, such as scurvy or vasculitis, can also lead to spontaneous bleeding despite normal platelet counts and clotting profiles. Identifying whether a bleeding disorder is inherited or acquired helps healthcare teams anticipate the clinical course, execute rapid diagnostic evaluations, and implement targeted therapeutic interventions to prevent life-threatening hemorrhages in vulnerable patients.

headings.title: Common Inherited Bleeding Disorders: Haemophilia and Von Willebrand Disease
headings.content: Inherited bleeding disorders present unique clinical and educational challenges for nursing professionals caring for patients in Nigeria. Haemophilia A and Haemophilia B are X-linked recessive bleeding disorders caused by deficiencies or functional defects in clotting factor VIII and factor IX, respectively. Because they are X-linked, they predominantly affect males, while females generally serve as asymptomatic carriers. Patients with haemophilia often experience spontaneous bleeding into large weight-bearing joints (hemarthrosis), deep muscles, and soft tissues, which can lead to chronic joint deformities and severe pain if left untreated. Von Willebrand disease (vWD), unlike haemophilia, is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and affects both males and females equally. It is caused by a deficiency or qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor, a crucial protein that mediates platelet adhesion to damaged vascular subendothelium and also acts as a carrier protein for factor VIII in the circulation. Clinical manifestations of vWD often include mucosal bleeding, such as frequent epistaxis, heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), and prolonged bleeding from minor cuts or dental procedures. Nursing management requires careful assessment for bleeding episodes, administration of factor concentrates or desmopressin as prescribed, and educating patients and families on safety precautions, joint protection, and avoidance of trauma or medications that inhibit platelet function, such as aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

headings.title: Acquired Bleeding Disorders: DIC and Vitamin K Deficiency
headings.content: Acquired bleeding disorders such as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and vitamin K deficiency are critical medical emergencies frequently managed in acute care units across Nigeria. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a complex, life-threatening syndrome triggered by an underlying systemic condition—such as severe sepsis, obstetric complications, trauma, or malignancy—which causes widespread activation of the clotting cascade. This massive intravascular clotting depletes circulating platelets and coagulation factors, paradoxically leading to both widespread microvascular thrombosis and severe, uncontrolled hemorrhage from surgical sites, venipuncture sites, and mucous membranes. Nursing care for DIC demands rigorous hemodynamic monitoring, rapid administration of blood products, fresh frozen plasma, and cryoprecipitate, alongside treating the root cause. On the other hand, vitamin K deficiency occurs when there is an inadequate intake, impaired intestinal absorption, or pharmacological antagonism of fat-soluble vitamin K. Vitamin K is essential for the hepatic synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. In adults, it can result from prolonged antibiotic therapy, malabsorption syndromes, or severe malnutrition. In neonates, vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) can occur due to low body stores at birth and sterile infant gut flora, making prophylactic vitamin K administration at birth a standard nursing intervention in Nigerian maternity wards. Treatment involves parenteral administration of vitamin K to rapidly restore clotting factor synthesis and halt bleeding.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Patient Assessment
headings.content: Clinical manifestations of bleeding disorders vary widely depending on whether the defect lies in primary haemostasis (platelets and blood vessels) or secondary haemostasis (coagulation factors). When conducting patient assessments in Nigerian clinical settings, nurses must recognize distinct clinical presentations. Primary haemostasis defects typically present with superficial bleeding manifestations, including petechiae (pinpoint purplish-red spots), purpura, ecchymoses (bruising), epistaxis (nosebleeds), gingival bleeding, and prolonged bleeding from minor skin cuts or menorrhagia. In contrast, secondary haemostasis defects, such as haemophilia, usually manifest as deeper tissue bleeding, including painful hemarthrosis (joint bleeding), deep muscle hematomas, retroperitoneal bleeds, and delayed bleeding following surgical or dental interventions. Comprehensive patient assessment requires taking a meticulous health and family history, inquiring about dietary habits, medication use (such as herbal remedies or NSAIDs), and recent illnesses. Physical examination must focus on evaluating skin integrity, checking mucous membranes, assessing joint range of motion for signs of hemarthrosis or swelling, and monitoring vital signs for early signs of hypovolemic shock, such as tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension. Continuous vigilance enables nurses to detect subtle signs of internal hemorrhage before hemodynamic instability ensues, ensuring prompt medical intervention.

headings.title: Diagnostic Investigations and Laboratory Tests
headings.content: Accurate diagnosis of bleeding disorders relies on a combination of thorough clinical evaluation and specialized laboratory investigations. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding these diagnostic tests is essential for interpreting lab reports and communicating critical findings to the medical team. Initial screening panels typically include a Complete Blood Count (CBC) with platelet count to evaluate primary haemostasis and check for thrombocytopenia. Coagulation profiles are vital for assessing secondary haemostasis: the Prothrombin Time (PT) and its standardized form, the International Normalized Ratio (INR), evaluate the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways (often used to monitor warfarin therapy), while the Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) assesses the intrinsic and common pathways (often used to monitor heparin therapy and diagnose haemophilia). Additional specialized investigations may include bleeding time or platelet function assays, fibrinogen levels, and D-dimer assays, which are particularly elevated in disseminated intravascular coagulation due to breakdown of cross-linked fibrin. Specific factor assays can also be performed to quantify the exact percentage activity of factor VIII, IX, or von Willebrand factor. Nurses play a crucial role in preparing patients for these tests, ensuring proper specimen collection techniques, avoiding contamination with heparin lines, and delivering blood samples to the laboratory promptly to ensure reliable results.

headings.title: Medical and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Medical and pharmacological management of bleeding disorders aims to correct the underlying deficiency, stop acute bleeding episodes, and prevent future complications. The treatment plan depends heavily on the specific disorder diagnosed. For inherited factor deficiencies like Haemophilia A and B, management centers on factor replacement therapy using recombinant or plasma-derived clotting factor concentrates infused intravenously. In emergency settings where factor concentrates are unavailable, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) or cryoprecipitate may be administered to supply missing clotting factors. Desmopressin (DDAVP), a synthetic analogue of vasopressin, can be used in mild Haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease to stimulate the release of stored factor VIII and von Willebrand factor from endothelial cells. For acquired disorders, such as vitamin K deficiency, parenteral vitamin K administration rapidly reverses coagulopathy. In cases of anticoagulant overdose, reversal agents such as prothrombin complex concentrate, fresh frozen plasma, or protamine sulfate (for heparin) are utilized. Furthermore, antifibrinolytic agents like tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid are frequently prescribed to prevent the premature breakdown of blood clots, especially during dental procedures or mucosal bleeding episodes. Nurses administering these pharmacological agents must monitor closely for adverse reactions, manage intravenous access carefully, and evaluate therapeutic efficacy by observing cessation of bleeding and improvements in coagulation lab profiles.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Patient Education
headings.content: Developing a comprehensive nursing care plan and providing effective patient education are paramount for improving the quality of life and survival rates of patients with bleeding disorders in Nigeria. The nursing care plan should prioritize safety, comfort, and prevention of hemorrhage. Key nursing diagnoses include risk for injury, acute pain related to hemarthrosis, and deficient knowledge regarding disease management. Nursing interventions involve implementing bleeding precautions: using soft-bristled toothbrushes, avoiding intramuscular injections, applying prolonged pressure (at least 5 to 10 minutes) to venipuncture sites, and eliminating contact sports or activities that risk trauma. Nurses must also manage acute joint pain by applying prescribed cold compresses, elevating affected limbs, and avoiding NSAIDs or aspirin, which impair platelet aggregation. Patient and family education is equally critical. Nurses must educate patients on recognizing early signs of bleeding (such as unexplained bruising, gum bleeding, dark stools, or joint warmth and swelling), adhering strictly to prescribed treatment regimens, and wearing medical alert identification bracelets. Furthermore, nurses should counsel patients to inform all healthcare providers, including traditional healers and dentists, of their bleeding disorder before undergoing any medical procedures, ensuring holistic, safe, and continuous patient-centered care.
